newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Korea's Hyundai plans $1.4 bln Scotland chip plant.
newsitem.headline: Korea's Hyundai plans $1.4 bln Scotland chip plant.

text.p: Hyundai Electronics, a unit of South Korea's sprawling Hyundai Group, said on Tuesday it planned a $1.4 billion semiconductor plant in Scotland to tap European markets with a new generation of computer memory chips.
"The main purpose of the project is securing a production base in Europe in order to expand our market share in the region and overcome trade barriers," a Hyundai spokesman said.
The plant would begin commercial production of dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips in December 1998 and generate about 1,000 jobs, he said.

Hyundai's plan came on the heels of LG Group's 1.7 billion stg deal in July to make semiconducters and electronic goods in Wales -- the biggest single overseas investment in Europe from outside the European region.

"Main items will be 64- and 256-megabit DRAMS, whose demand in Europe is expected to rise sharply from late next year on," he said. The 64-megabit and faster 256-megabit chips are considered a new generation in semiconductor products.

Prices for widely-used 16-megabit DRAM chips have slumped following a huge glut of supply, weighing heavily on South Korea's electronics firms and forcing them to look further abroad for new investment opportunities, analysts said.
The move to produce faster memory chips is particularly important for the South Korean economy, whose exports have been hit hard by spiralling prices for the 16-megabit chips.

The Scotland plant would be Hyundai Electronics' first ever European investment. The group began construction in February on a $1.3 billion semiconductor plant in the United States which is due to be completed late next year.
Hyundai said it selected Dunfermline, about 24 km (15 miles) north of Edinburgh, because of various favourable conditions which Britain offered.

"We also thought of other regions in Britain, Ireland and Spain as candidates for our investment. But Scotland was the best in terms of securing manpower and technology related to semiconductor production," the spokesman said.

Michael Forsyth, Scotland's Secretary of State said: "Our low-tax, low-inflation economy combined with our skilled and flexible workfoce have made us the envy of Europe. Hyundai's investment represents a major vote of confidence in Scotland."
Analysts said Hyundai was well positioned to tap the European markets, which already rely heavily on South Korea and Japan for supplies of semiconductors.
"It would be advantageous to have a large-scale factory in Europe because there are no major semiconductor producers there," said Koo Hee-jin, an analyst at Daishin Securities.

He said Europe, which currently lags the United States in use of personal computers, can provide a huge market for memory chips as demand there increases, especially considering the European region's well-developed economies.
By advancing to Europe, Hyundai would be able to learn advanced design know-how on non-memory chips such as application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs).

"Hyundai's investment in Europe looks appropriate in that local production would allow Hyundai to quickly respond to changes in market conditions and to save transportation costs," said one analyst at a research institute.
In a similar move, LG Group said in July it would pour huge money into building plants in Newport, Wales, for production of semiconductors, monitors and colour picture tubes.
When completed in 2002, the LG plants will create more than 6,000 jobs for Britain.
